core.text: Latin says who goes along with whom by putting *cum* in front of **the ablative (the 'with someone' form)**, *ablātīvus sociātīvus*: *cum Mārcō* — with Marcus; *cum ancillīs* — with the maidservants; *cum cane et ovibus* — with his dog and his sheep. The companion is usually a person, sometimes an animal or something carried along. *Cum* is the only preposition that does this, and it never drops out: no *cum*, no company.

*With* does two jobs in English: the one you are alongside (*he walked with Davus*) and the thing you use (*he cut it with a knife*). Latin keeps the two apart, and only the first gets a word for *with*.
Company: *cum* + ablative (*cum Dāvō*). A thing you use: the bare ablative, no preposition at all (*gladiō*).

invented.la: Vir cum gladiō in viā stat.
invented.en: A man is standing in the street with a sword (carrying one).

core.text: *Vir cum gladiō stat* is a man carrying a sword; *vir gladiō pugnat* is a man using one. Test it with *and*: if you could write *Mārcus et Dāvus ambulant* instead, it is company and *cum* stays. If the noun is the thing that does the work, drop *cum* and let the bare ending say it. Ørberg never writes *cum* for a tool.

The same three letters are also a conjunction. *Cum Dāvō ambulat* — *cum* with a noun in the ablative: with Davus. *Cum ambulāret* — *cum* with a verb: when he was walking. Look at the word after *cum*: a noun in the ablative means company, a verb means a clause has started.

more.text: The learner's notes teach *cum* on the same two pages as *in* and *sub* (p15–16), because all three ask for the same case. The question they answer is not the same: *in vīllā* answers *ubi?* — where?, *cum Aemiliā* answers *quōcum?* — with whom? Its opposite is *sine* + ablative (*sine Aemiliā* — without Aemilia, r05:45.2), which takes the ablative for the same reason.

A personal or relative pronoun takes *cum* glued on behind it: *mēcum*, *tēcum*, *sēcum*, *nōbīscum*, *vōbīscum*, *quōcum* — never *cum mē*. *Ūnā cum* is the same construction with an adverb in front, 'together with' (*ūnā cum Iūliā*, r20:103.1). Verbs of fighting and talking keep the company sense: *pugnāvimus cum puerō māiōre* — we fought with (against) a bigger boy (r21:45.1); *cum Aemiliā colloquitur* — she talks with Aemilia. A&G §413 (accompaniment), §409 (means).
